Learning Objectives
  1. Identify and discuss the clinical presentation and diagnosis of acne vulgaris, rosacea, and hidradenitis suppurativa, and explain how their treatments vary.
  2. Identify and discuss the clinical presentation, diagnosis, and treatment of hyperhidrosis.
  3. Identify and discuss the clinical presentation and diagnosis of common disorders of pigment such as vitiligo, pityriasis alba, and tinea versicolor, including approaches to therapy.
  4. Identify and discuss the clinical presentation, diagnosis, pathophysiology, and treatment of common hair disorders such as alopecia areata, tinea capitis, telogen effluvium, and androgenic alopecia.
Big Picture

This lecture is best learned as a set of morphology → mechanism → distribution → treatment patterns. Start by naming what you see, then ask what process creates it, where it prefers to occur, and which treatment attacks that mechanism.

Morphology→Distribution→Mechanism→Diagnosis→Treatment
Learning Objective 1

Acneiform disorders

Acne vulgaris, rosacea, and hidradenitis suppurativa can all produce inflammatory papules or nodules, but their defining morphology, anatomic distribution, and pathogenesis are different.

MUST KNOW

Acne vulgaris: the comedone is the anchor

Acne is common in adolescence and can persist through the 20s and 30s. Typical sites are the face, chest, and back. The lecture's diagnostic anchor is the presence of comedones, often accompanied by papules and pustules.

Follicular hyperkeratinization + sebum → follicular plugging / microcomedone → open or closed comedone → bacterial proliferation + inflammation → papules, pustules, nodules/cysts → possible scarring

The pathogenesis diagram emphasizes excess keratin cohesiveness in the follicle, androgen-stimulated sebum production, comedone formation, and inflammatory change associated with Propionibacterium acnes in the lecture's terminology.

FIRST AID CONNECTION

What First Aid adds: acne is multifactorial: increased sebum/androgen activity, abnormal keratinocyte desquamation, Cutibacterium acnes colonization, and inflammation. The name Cutibacterium acnes is the current name for the organism called Propionibacterium acnes on the course slides.

Why it matters: each treatment category maps to one or more of these mechanisms.

Acne severity → treatment ladder

PatternClinical morphologyCourse treatmentMechanistic logic
ComedonalOpen/closed comedones; mildest formTopical retinoids: tretinoin, tazarotene, adapaleneNormalize follicular keratinization → less plugging and fewer comedones. Lecture notes ≥6 weeks for effect.
Mild inflammatoryPapules/pustules + comedones; none to few deep nodulesTretinoin/adapalene + topical antibiotics and/or benzoyl peroxide; clindamycin or erythromycin; benzoyl peroxide wash 4–6%Retinoid addresses plugging; antimicrobial therapy targets acne-associated bacteria.
Moderate inflammatoryTender nodules + comedones + papules + pustulesTretinoin + benzoyl peroxide wash + oral antibiotic; lecture example: doxycycline 100 mg BIDMore inflammatory burden → add systemic anti-inflammatory/antimicrobial therapy.
Hormonal pattern in femalesMay flare before menses; often chin/jawlineOral contraceptive pills or spironolactoneSpironolactone is anti-androgenic and alters hormone-driven sebum production.
NodulocysticMany deep nodules/cysts with inflammatory papules/pustules; high scarring riskMay use antibiotics + topicals, but many patients require isotretinoinIsotretinoin induces sebocyte apoptosis and normalizes keratinization; course also notes decreased P. acnes.
MUST KNOW

Isotretinoin

Course: typically a 6–8 month weight-based course to a goal dose; monitor LFTs, lipids, and monthly pregnancy testing. The lecture lists dryness of skin/mucosa, photosensitivity, inflammatory bowel disease, hair loss, joint pain, depression, LFT/triglyceride elevations, and severe birth defects among adverse effects.

Course priority: it is highly effective and a severe teratogen requiring iPLEDGE monitoring.

LECTURE → STEP 1 BRIDGE

Lecture: severe nodulocystic acne → isotretinoin. First Aid: isotretinoin is a vitamin A derivative; vitamin A excess patterns include dry skin, alopecia, hepatotoxicity, arthralgias, increased intracranial pressure, and teratogenicity. How Step 1 may test it: reproductive counseling or toxicity clues in a patient on therapy for severe cystic acne.

Post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation

Course: common with all acne types, worse in darker skin types, and worsened by picking/popping. Management centers on time, prevention of new lesions, and sunscreen; fading may take months.

CLINICAL CONNECTION

Control of active inflammation is also prevention of future pigment change and scar formation. That is why “treat the acne” and “treat the sequela” are not separate problems.

Retrieval Checkpoint · Why is a comedone such a useful discriminator?
Because the lecture defines acne vulgaris by comedones. Rosacea can have inflammatory papules/pustules but specifically lacks comedones, so comedones push the diagnosis toward acne.

Rosacea: inflammation + neurovascular dysregulation, but no comedones

The lecture frames rosacea as an inflammatory disorder involving immune and neurovascular dysregulation, with a possible exaggerated immune response to Demodex. Genetic predisposition and triggers such as alcohol, sun, and spicy foods contribute to flushing/sensitivity and inflammatory papules/pustules.

EXAM TRAP

Rosacea papules/pustules are not acne. The course explicitly emphasizes no comedones.

SubtypeRecognitionCourse treatment
ErythematotelangiectaticFacial erythema + telangiectasias; burning/flushing sensitivityAvoid triggers, sunscreen, gentle skin care, pulsed dye laser, beta blockers for flushing, topical α2 agonist (brimonidine) → vasoconstriction
PapulopustularCentral facial erythematous papules/pustules on background erythemaSunscreen/gentle care, trigger avoidance, topical metronidazole (anti-inflammatory), topical ivermectin (targets Demodex), low-dose doxycycline (anti-inflammatory)
PhymatousLongstanding inflammation → sebaceous gland hypertrophy + fibrosis; classically men/noseSurgical excision or ablative laser
OcularBlepharitis, eyelid swelling, conjunctival injection, dry eyes, frequent blinkingArtificial tears + low-dose doxycycline
Retrieval Checkpoint · A patient has central facial erythema, papules and pustules. What single finding would argue against acne?
Absence of comedones strongly supports rosacea in the lecture's framework.

Hidradenitis suppurativa: follicular occlusion → sterile abscesses → sinus tracts → scars

Also called acne inversa. The lecture describes an unknown trigger causing occlusion of pilosebaceous units in skin with apocrine glands, followed by inflammation, painful nodules/sterile abscesses, draining sinus tracts, and scarring.

MUST KNOW

Who / where: begins at or soon after puberty; females more than males; lecture notes higher prevalence in African Americans than Caucasians. Obesity and tobacco use are risk factors. Sites are intertriginous: axillae, inframammary folds, groin, and buttocks.

Intertriginous site + recurrent painful nodules/abscesses → look for sinus tracts/scars → Hurley stage → escalate treatment
HIGH YIELD

All stages: weight loss and smoking cessation are part of treatment. Early treatment matters because the disease is chronic/progressive and can become painful, disfiguring, and malodorous.

Hurley stageMorphologyCourse treatment
IInflammatory nodules and sterile abscesses; no sinus tracts or scarsTopical antibiotics, antiseptic washes, intralesional steroids, oral antibiotics (rifampin + clindamycin, doxycycline) for anti-inflammatory effects
IIInflammatory nodules/abscesses + few sinus tracts and scarsOral antibiotics; spironolactone or finasteride (anti-androgen effects); adalimumab; surgical excision
IIIMultiple interconnected sinus tracts + scarring, often covering an entire regionLecture groups biologic therapy including adalimumab, infliximab, and secukinumab and references TNF-α / IL-17 targets; surgical excision
Retrieval Checkpoint · What feature upgrades Hurley I to Hurley II?
The appearance of sinus tracts and scars. Stage I has none; stage II has a few; stage III has multiple interconnected tracts with extensive scarring.
Learning Objective 2

Hyperhidrosis

First decide whether sweating is primary focal disease or secondary to another condition or medication.

Primary vs secondary

PrimarySecondary
No underlying disease; lecture notes ~80% family history; palms, soles, axillae are typical.Related to disease or medication. Lecture examples: febrile illness, hyperthyroidism, lymphoma/other cancer, amphetamines, insulin, sulfonylureas, SSRIs, opioids.
MUST KNOW · Diagnostic Pattern

The criteria shown in the lecture image are: focal visible excessive sweating ≥6 months with no apparent secondary cause, plus at least two of the following: bilateral/symmetric, impairs daily activities, ≥1 episode/week, onset before age 25, positive family history, or stops during sleep.

Treatment mechanisms

  • Aluminum chloride 12–20% (DrySol): physically occludes eccrine sweat glands.
  • Glycopyrrolate / oxybutynin: anticholinergics that block muscarinic receptors on eccrine sweat glands.
  • Botulinum toxin: blocks acetylcholine release; lecture notes repeated treatment about every 6–9 months.
Retrieval Checkpoint · What historical clue should make you reconsider “primary” hyperhidrosis?
A secondary cause such as fever, hyperthyroidism, malignancy, or a medication associated with sweating.
Learning Objective 3

Pigmentary disorders

The practical distinction is true depigmentation versus hypopigmented patches with scale or an atopic context.

DisorderMorphology / distributionMechanism / associationsCourse therapy
VitiligoDepigmented patches; hands, feet, perioral and periocular skin commonly affectedAutoimmunity targeting melanocytes; associated with alopecia areata, autoimmune hypothyroidism, Graves diseaseTopical steroids, narrow-band UVB, ruxolitinib
Pityriasis albaHypopigmented round patches with slight scale on face of young childrenOften in children with atopic dermatitis; may be a mild variant; can look more obvious in summerBenign, resolves with age; moisturizers or 1% hydrocortisone for dry appearance
Tinea versicolorMost often hypopigmented patches on chest/back in teens/young adultsOvergrowth of Malassezia yeast; lecture says yeast decreases melanin synthesis/tanning, so contrast worsens in summerTopical azoles, fluconazole, or OTC dandruff shampoo
FIRST AID CONNECTION

Vitiligo: First Aid reinforces autoimmune melanocyte destruction and association with other autoimmune disease. Tinea versicolor: First Aid adds the classic “spaghetti and meatballs” microscopy pattern and explains that Malassezia-derived acids inhibit tyrosinase, reducing melanin synthesis.

COMMON CONFUSION

Vitiligo = complete depigmentation from melanocyte destruction. Pityriasis alba = mildly scaly hypopigmented facial patches in children. Tinea versicolor = yeast-associated patches, usually trunk/back, especially visible in summer.

Retrieval Checkpoint · Child with subtle scaly facial hypopigmentation vs teenager with multiple trunk patches: which is which?
Child + facial + slight scale/atopy → pityriasis alba. Teen/young adult + chest/back + Malassezia pattern → tinea versicolor.
Learning Objective 4

Disorders of hair

Sort hair loss by pattern: focal smooth, focal scaly/itchy, diffuse sudden shedding, or patterned miniaturization.

Alopecia areata

  • Common, non-scarring alopecia affecting all ages/races; often positive family history and often affects children/young adults.
  • Circular smooth areas of hair loss with no erythema or scale; usually asymptomatic.
  • Pathophysiology: T-cell-mediated autoimmune destruction of hair follicles.
  • Totalis = all scalp hair; universalis = all body hair.
  • Associations: atopy, Hashimoto thyroiditis, vitiligo.
  • Localized treatment: topical/intralesional corticosteroids, topical calcineurin inhibitors. Widespread/rapidly progressive: oral steroids or tofacitinib per lecture.
  • Course prognosis: usually self-resolves within ~6 months; localized disease often responds; recurrence can occur; extensive disease is more treatment-resistant.
CLINICAL CONNECTION

Smooth skin without scale argues for alopecia areata rather than fungal infection.

Tinea capitis

Dermatophyte fungal infection of hair follicles can mimic alopecia areata. The lecture tells you to separate them using scale and itching. Diagnosis can be made by scraping with microscopic examination or fungal culture.

Course treatment is oral antifungal therapy such as terbinafine, griseofulvin, or fluconazole for 4–8 weeks.

HIGH YIELD

Hair-follicle infection requires systemic therapy in the lecture — do not treat this as a simple smooth patch of alopecia.

LECTURE → STEP 1 BRIDGE

Lecture: scaly/itchy focal alopecia → scrape/culture → oral antifungal. Step 1 move: use surface scale and fungal evidence to distinguish infection from autoimmune alopecia.

Telogen effluvium vs androgenic alopecia

FeatureTelogen effluviumAndrogenic alopecia
PatternDiffuse, sudden sheddingPatterned progressive loss
Trigger / mechanismIllness, hospitalization, pregnancy, surgery, or other stress → more rapid hair cycling and increased sheddingCirculating androgens → progressive follicular miniaturization
CourseSelf-resolves in 6–12 monthsOften familial and progressive
Sex-pattern clueNo sex-specific patterned distribution taughtMen: frontal/vertex loss. Women: widening of the part line.
TreatmentLecture emphasizes spontaneous resolutionTopical minoxidil + anti-androgens such as finasteride, spironolactone, dutasteride

The normal hair cycle is anagen (growth) → catagen (regression) → telogen (rest). The lecture uses ~100 hairs/day as a normal-loss anchor. Telogen effluvium shifts more hairs into shedding after a stressor.

FIRST AID CONNECTION

First Aid reinforces the DHT mechanism: testosterone → DHT via 5α-reductase; DHT contributes to androgenetic alopecia. Finasteride inhibits 5α-reductase. First Aid also lists minoxidil for androgenetic alopecia.

Retrieval Checkpoint · Four patients: smooth circular patch, scaly itchy patch, diffuse shedding after surgery, widening part line. Match the diagnoses.
Smooth circular patch → alopecia areata. Scaly itchy patch → tinea capitis. Diffuse shedding after surgery → telogen effluvium. Widening part line → female-pattern androgenic alopecia.
End-of-Lecture Synthesis

MASTER THESE BEFORE MOVING ON

1 · Morphology firstComedones identify acne; rosacea has papules/pustules without comedones; hidradenitis is deep intertriginous nodules/abscesses with tract/scar progression.
2 · Treatment should follow mechanism and severityTopical retinoid for comedonal acne → antimicrobial/anti-inflammatory escalation → isotretinoin for severe nodulocystic disease; rosacea/HS use different ladders.
3 · Pigment language mattersVitiligo is depigmentation from melanocyte destruction; pityriasis alba and tinea versicolor are hypopigmented patterns with scale/context clues.
4 · Hair-loss pattern is the diagnostic shortcutSmooth focal = alopecia areata; scaly focal = tinea capitis; diffuse after stress = telogen effluvium; patterned = androgenic alopecia.
5 · Recognize long-term consequencesSevere acne scars; hidradenitis creates sinus tracts/scarring; early adequate treatment matters because structural change is harder to reverse.
THE MOST USEFUL FIRST AID CONNECTIONS
  1. Acne → isotretinoin: vitamin A derivative, strong teratogenicity/toxicity connection.
  2. Vitiligo: autoimmune destruction of melanocytes; autoimmune associations reinforce the lecture.
  3. Tinea versicolor: Malassezia with the classic “spaghetti and meatballs” microscopy pattern.
  4. Androgenic alopecia: DHT-driven follicular miniaturization; finasteride blocks 5α-reductase, and minoxidil is a treatment.
  5. Dermatology vocabulary: precise lesion terms such as papule and pustule improve vignette recognition.
